title: Pwn2Own Ireland Day 1: AI infrastructure falls as 32 zero-days hit Cork stage
subtitle: LiteLLM, OpenAI Codex, and Oracle's Autonomous AI Database were all demonstrated against on the opening day of the Zero Day Initiative contest, which paid out $388,500 before lunch on day two.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Zero Day Initiative's Pwn2Own Ireland 2026 contest opened in Cork on October 6, and researchers moved through 32 previously undisclosed vulnerabilities on day one for a combined $388,500 in payouts. The event's AI Infrastructure and AI Coding Agents categories — both new or expanded for this year's contest — produced demonstrated exploits against LiteLLM, OpenAI's Codex cloud agent, and Oracle's Autonomous AI Database. The Samsung Galaxy S26 was taken down twice. VinSOC earned $40,000 for a five-bug exploit chain against the Oracle AI Database, and a separate team used a single argument-injection flaw to compromise Codex.

The specific LiteLLM bugs have not been published; under Pwn2Own's disclosure terms the vendors have 90 days to issue patches before the Zero Day Initiative releases full write-ups. The pattern is already visible, though. LiteLLM also fell at Pwn2Own Berlin in May, where k3vg3n chained three bugs — a server-side request forgery, a code-injection path, and a trust-boundary failure — to take over the proxy. OpenAI's Codex was exploited at Berlin as well, by Sina Kheirkhah of Summoning Team for $20,000. Two consecutive contests at the same AI tools is not a one-off result.

The broader read is that the AI tool chain is now a mainstream target with mainstream economics. Pwn2Own does not pay out for theoretical attacks or impressive-looking demos; the exploits have to work live against the current shipping build, in front of judges, inside a strict time window. Oracle's AI Database joining phones, printers, and smart-home hubs as a Pwn2Own target is the clearest sign yet that AI-adjacent infrastructure is being treated the same way enterprise databases, hypervisors, and operating systems have been treated for the last decade — as surface area that attackers can plan a career around and defenders have to budget for. The $40,000 Oracle payout is small compared to the cleanup cost of a chained exploit landing in production.

A takeaway for learners: the fastest way to understand AI security is to read a Pwn2Own schedule and then look at what wins. Argument injection against an AI coding agent is not an exotic attack; it is the agent trusting user-supplied text, then passing it to a shell or an API call without a strict boundary. SSRF against a model proxy is the proxy fetching a URL the attacker controls. The lesson for anyone shipping an LLM-backed app is the same lesson that web developers learned about SQL injection in 2005: every string that crosses a trust boundary needs an owner, a type, and a check — and the places you have not thought carefully about those three things are where the next $40,000 payout will come from.
